title: Documentation
text:
The use of custom RNA-seq derived protein sequences has been shown to be a viable strategy for identifying non-canonical gene products not documented in common protein sequence databases. However, the inclusion of too many sequences can lead to false positive identifications. JCAST combines splice junction modeling and one-frame translation to create small custom protein sequence databases.
JCAST is a command line tool that takes an annotation GTF file, rMATS results, and a genome FASTA file to create custom protein FASTA files for downstream analysis. To prioritize likely detectable splice junctions, JCAST can model the splice junction read counts in RNA-seq (-m) and use this model to calculate the minimal read count cutoff for in silico translation. Without -m, the cutoff is set with -r (by default 1, which keeps every junction). An example of the read count mixture model is shown below.

title: Documentation
text:
Output
JCAST outputs FASTA databases which can be further filtered and combined using any scripting language, or used directly in virtually any shotgun proteomics database search engine (e.g., SEQUEST, Crux/Tide, MaxQuant, MS-GF+). Depending on the settings and input files, not every file below is written.
JCAST writes a small number of FASTA files into the output directory. Each entry’s header encodes the source rMATS row, slice number, junction coordinates, translation strand, frame, and tier (see below).







File
Contents




psq_canonical.fasta
Sequences identical to the canonical SwissProt/GTF protein for the gene. Headers follow UniProt convention.


psq_T1.fasta
Tier 1. Both slices translate in their annotated reading frames with no premature stop codon (PTC), and the event does not shift the reading frame: the slices’ coding lengths, measured from each slice’s frame, differ by a multiple of 3. Both slices are stitched into the canonical full-length protein.


psq_T1_alt_cterm.fasta
Tier 1, alternative C-terminus. One slice ends at an annotated protein-coding stop codon that is not the canonical protein’s. It is a complete C-terminus, not a premature stop, and is joined to the canonical at its N-terminus only.


psq_T1_alt_nterm.fasta
Tier 1, alternative N-terminus. The gene’s start codon lies in an alternative exon that this slice lacks. The slice is translated from another annotated start codon it contains, and joined to the canonical at its C-terminus only.


psq_T1_alt_both.fasta
Tier 1, both termini alternative. The slice starts at an alternative annotated start codon and ends at an alternative annotated stop codon (created only when needed).


psq_T2.fasta
Tier 2. As T1, but the coding lengths differ by a non-multiple of 3 (frameshift). A slice that cannot be stitched at both ends may be joined at its N-terminus only.


psq_T4.fasta
Tier 4. Only one slice translates; the other hits a PTC. The PTC slice is translated up to its stop codon, giving a truncated product, which is joined to the canonical at its N-terminus. If it is shorter than params.ptc_threshold × the other slice, or cannot be joined, it goes to psq_T4_orphan.fasta. Treat T4 with caution — exclude from MS searches unless you have a specific reason to include it.


psq_T#_orphan.fasta
Slices of that tier that translated but could not be stitched back to the canonical sequence: no unique 7-residue anchor at an end that needs joining. Treat orphans with caution.


uniprot_canonicals.tsv
With --uniprot: the canonical chosen for each gene, and how (by sequence, by gene name, from the GTF, or none).


psq_isoforms.tsv
With --uniprot: every JCAST record identical to a UniProt canonical or isoform, with its accession.


jcast_uniprot_merged.fasta
With --uniprot: a search database, made of the supplied UniProt FASTA plus the new psq_T1 and psq_T1_alt_* records, renamed sp|<accession>-J<n>|<entry name>.


junctions.tsv
One row per junction, in rMATS file order: its read count, FDR, fate, frames, coding region, canonical, and the files its records went to. See below.


logfile.log
The run’s settings and inputs, warnings and errors, and a summary: junctions by fate and splice type, records per file, and the time taken. With -v, also each junction’s steps and sequences.









Warning



Note: Tier 4 and orphan sequences are truncated or not full-length. Exclude them from database searches, or interpret them with a great amount of caution.


There is no Tier 3 from v0.4.0. It re-translated in a guessed frame when the annotated frame failed, and was removed together with the three-frame fallback (see CHANGELOG.md).
Annotated start and stop codons are taken from protein-coding transcripts with transcript support level ≤ params.tsl_threshold. A stop codon annotated only on nonsense-mediated-decay transcripts, or not annotated at all, is still a premature stop (T4).
How a junction is processed (v0.4.0):

Filters. A junction whose read count (header field 11) is below the cutoff, or whose rMATS FDR is outside -q, is skipped before anything else. The cutoff is -r, or the -m model’s boundary in reads; a junction with exactly that many reads is kept. With -c, a skipped junction’s gene still gets its canonical written.
Trimming. Every exon is trimmed to the gene’s annotated coding region. This runs from the most upstream start codon to the most distal stop codon of protein-coding transcripts with transcript support level ≤ params.tsl_threshold. Exons entirely in the UTR are removed.
Skip if outside the coding region. If the splice event lies entirely outside the coding region, both slices are identical after trimming. The junction is skipped (SKIPPED. Splice event lies outside the annotated coding region.), and the canonical is still written with -c.
Reading frame. Each slice is read in its own frame, taken from the annotated coding sequence at the slice’s 5′ end. A slice with no annotated frame is not translated, for example in a lncRNA or a pseudogene. Frames are never guessed.

Skipped and failed junctions write no isoform sequences. Each junction’s outcome (fate) is a row of junctions.tsv.
For a typical proteomics workflow, append psq_T1.fasta and psq_canonical.fasta to a base SwissProt database and search as usual. Including T2, T4 and orphans is possible but increases false-discovery risk.

junctions.tsv
One row per junction of the selected splice types, in rMATS file order, tab-separated. It reads directly into R (read.delim) or pandas (pd.read_table).







Column
Contents




junction_type, junction_id
The rMATS splice type and row id.


gene_id, gene_symbol, chr, strand
As in the rMATS row.


min_jc
The read count that -r and -m filter on (header field 11).


fdr
The rMATS FDR, which -q filters on.


fate
T1, T1_alt_terminus, T2, T4, fail (no slice translates), exception (the junction raised an error; see the log), skipped_low_count, skipped_fdr, skipped_masked or skipped_outside_cds.


fate_detail
For T4, the slice that hit the premature stop; for exception, the error.


slice1_phase, slice2_phase
Each slice’s annotated frame (0, 1 or 2). Empty if it has none, or if the junction was skipped before it was looked up.


cds_start, cds_end
The coding region the slices were trimmed to. Empty if unknown on that side, or not looked up.


canonical_source, canonical_accession
Where the gene’s canonical came from: as in uniprot_canonicals.tsv with --uniprot (e.g. sp by sequence), sp by API or tr by API without it, gtf, or none. Empty if it was not looked up (a skipped junction without -c).


files
The psq_<name>.fasta files of the junction’s records, as <name>, ;-separated.


new_records
How many of its records were written. A record whose sequence is already in its file, from an earlier junction, is not written again.





Header format
Non-canonical FASTA entries are named as follows:
>sp|Q91VW5|GOGA4_MOUSE|ENSMUSG00000038708|MXE1|0|chr9|118560742:118560872|118565557:118565667|+2|r521|T1 sp|Q91VW5|...
The |-separated fields are:

Knowledgebase code (sp for SwissProt).
UniProt accession of the canonical entry.
UniProt entry name.
Ensembl gene id.
rMATS splice type and slice number (e.g. MXE1, MXE2).
rMATS row id.
Chromosome.
Anchor exon start:end.
Alternative exon start:end.
Translated strand and that slice’s phase (e.g. +2).
Read count, prefixed with r: the smaller of the junction’s inclusion and skipping junction counts, each summed over samples and replicates. This is the count -r and -m filter on.
Tier (T1, T1_alt_cterm, T1_alt_nterm, T1_alt_both, T2, T4).

When the canonical comes from the GTF rather than UniProt (use_gtf_only in jcast/params.py, or a gene without a UniProt entry with --uniprot), fields 1–3 are the Ensembl gene id, the gene symbol, and the gene id again. A gene that rMATS reports without a symbol (NA) is named NoGeneName_<gene id>.

title: Documentation
text:
Options
$ jcast --help
usage: jcast [-h] [-o OUT] [--overwrite] [--cache_dir CACHE_DIR] [-r READ] [-m] [-c]
             [--uniprot UNIPROT] [-p PROCESSES] [-v] [--mask MASK]
             [-s {MXE,SE,RI,A5SS,A3SS} [{MXE,SE,RI,A5SS,A3SS} ...]] [-q q_lo q_hi]
             rmats_folder gtf_file genome

jcast retrieves transcript splice junctionsand translates them into amino acid sequences

positional arguments:
  rmats_folder          path to folder storing rMATS output
  gtf_file              path to Ensembl gtf file
  genome                path to genome file (optionally .gz)

options:
  -h, --help            show this help message and exit
  -o OUT, --out OUT     output directory, created if needed [default: out]
  --overwrite           replace the output of an earlier run in the output directory; without it,
                        a directory holding JCAST output is refused [default: False]
  --cache_dir CACHE_DIR
                        directory for the GTF cache and the UniProt API cache [default: the user
                        cache directory, e.g. ~/Library/Caches/jcast or ~/.cache/jcast]
  -r READ, --read READ  the lowest read count for a junction to be translated: the smaller of its
                        inclusion and skipping junction counts, each summed over samples and
                        replicates [default: 1, which keeps every junction]
  -m, --model           take the read count cutoff from a Gamma + Normal mixture model of the read
                        counts of every rMATS file in the folder (also those -s leaves out),
                        instead of -r (used only if the fit fails) [default: False]
  -c, --canonical       write out canonical protein sequence even if transcriptslices are
                        untranslatable [default: False]
  --uniprot UNIPROT     UniProt FASTA (e.g. Swiss-Prot with isoforms for the species, optionally
                        .gz) to take canonical proteins from instead of the UniProt API; genes
                        without an entry use the GTF. Also writes jcast_uniprot_merged.fasta,
                        psq_isoforms.tsv and uniprot_canonicals.tsv [default: none, use the API]
  -p PROCESSES, --processes PROCESSES
                        number of processes to translate junctions in; the output is the same for
                        any number. More than 1 needs --uniprot (canonicals from the UniProt API
                        are fetched and cached by one process only), and macOS or Linux [default:
                        1]
  -v, --verbose         also log each junction's steps and its sequences, at DEBUG level (large:
                        300 MB for a whole-genome -m run); without it, the log has the run's
                        settings, warnings, errors and a summary, and each junction's outcome is
                        in junctions.tsv [default: False]
  --mask MASK           deprecated and ignored: slices containing any base other than A, C, G or T
                        (case-insensitive) are always skipped. Will be removed in the next
                        release.
  -s {MXE,SE,RI,A5SS,A3SS} [{MXE,SE,RI,A5SS,A3SS} ...], --splice_type {MXE,SE,RI,A5SS,A3SS} [{MXE,SE,RI,A5SS,A3SS} ...]
                        splice types to translate; only their rMATS files need to be in the folder
                        [default: MXE SE RI A5SS A3SS]
  -q q_lo q_hi, --qvalue q_lo q_hi
                        take junctions with rMATS fdr within this threshold [default: 0 1]

Canonicals from a UniProt FASTA (--uniprot, recommended)
By default JCAST asks the UniProt API for each gene’s canonical protein. If a request fails after its retries, or is refused, that junction fails (FAILURE (exception), see below) rather than going on without a canonical, and the run continues. With --uniprot, JCAST reads a UniProt FASTA you supply instead. This needs no network access, and the file records which UniProt release was used. Download Swiss-Prot with isoforms for your species, for human:
curl -o uniprot_sprot_human_isoforms_2026_04.fasta.gz \
  'https://rest.uniprot.org/uniprotkb/stream?compressed=true&format=fasta&includeIsoform=true&query=(proteome:UP000005640)+AND+(reviewed:true)'
Put the release in the file name, as above. The FASTA itself does not record it; the download’s X-UniProt-Release response header does.
Each gene’s canonical is chosen as follows: 1. the UniProt canonical whose sequence equals a protein translated from one of the gene’s GTF transcripts; 2. else the one whose gene name (GN=) is the gene symbol, if no other gene in the GTF has that symbol; 3. else the GTF canonical.
A match is used only if it is unique. No identifiers are mapped: GTFs carry no UniProt accessions. On a whole human genome this agrees with UniProt’s own Ensembl cross-references for 99.35% of protein-coding genes that have a Swiss-Prot entry (reports/2026-11-12-uniprot-mapping-audit.md).
The GTF canonical is the longest coding sequence among the gene’s protein-coding transcripts that have transcript support level ≤ params.tsl_threshold (2) and annotated start and stop codons. If none qualifies, it is the transcript the GTF tags Ensembl_canonical, as GENCODE GTFs do, at any support level, if: - it is protein-coding; - it has annotated start and stop codons; - it is not tagged readthrough_transcript.
Readthrough genes get no GTF canonical unless one of their transcripts passes the first rule. - A readthrough transcript spans two neighbouring genes. - rMATS reports each event under one gene only. In a whole-genome human run, 45% of the readthrough genes’ skipped-exon events skip an exon of another protein-coding gene. - Joined to a readthrough canonical, their slices would read as fusion proteins, so they are written as orphans (_orphan files). - In that run (GENCODE v50, Swiss-Prot), 370 of the 371 protein-coding genes left without a canonical are readthrough genes (reports/2026-11-12-ensembl-canonical-audit.md).
Swiss-Prot or Swiss-Prot + TrEMBL. - For human, Swiss-Prot is recommended. - A FASTA that also holds TrEMBL entries (reviewed:false) is accepted. TrEMBL entries are used only after Swiss-Prot, by the same rules. - Adding TrEMBL gives a canonical to some genes that have neither a Swiss-Prot entry nor a GTF canonical. In a whole human genome that is 203 genes. Their records can then be joined instead of written as orphans. - For species with little Swiss-Prot coverage, include TrEMBL. - Records joined to a TrEMBL canonical are named tr|…. They are left out of jcast_uniprot_merged.fasta, which merges Swiss-Prot only.
The run also writes: - uniprot_canonicals.tsv: the canonical chosen per gene, and how. - psq_isoforms.tsv: every JCAST record identical to a UniProt canonical or isoform. - jcast_uniprot_merged.fasta: a search database. It holds every entry of the supplied FASTA, then each psq_T1 and psq_T1_alt_* record that was joined to a Swiss-Prot canonical and is not identical to a UniProt entry. Each is renamed sp|<accession>-J<n>|<entry name>, followed by its JCAST header.


Several processes (-p)
-p N translates junctions in N processes. The output files and the log are the same as with one process (except for the run time): - the worker processes only translate; - the main process writes every record, row of junctions.tsv and log line in rMATS file order.
On a whole-genome run, 16 processes are about 11× faster than one. Memory barely grows, because the workers share the genome and GTF already loaded rather than copying them.
-p above 1 has two requirements: - --uniprot. Without it, canonicals come from the UniProt API, one request per gene. The answers are cached in a local database that several processes cannot safely share, and concurrent requests would load the EBI servers. The command line rejects -p 2 without --uniprot. - macOS or Linux. On Windows, JCAST warns and uses one process.
Leave a core or two for the system: -p set to the number of cores minus 2 is a reasonable maximum.

title: Documentation
text:
Known issues

Use an unmasked or soft-masked genome, not a hard-masked one.

Soft-masked (lowercase) bases are read as ordinary sequence, so Ensembl dna_sm or UCSC hg38.fa give exactly the same output as an unmasked genome.
Any slice containing N or another ambiguous base is skipped (fate SKIPPED ... masked or ambiguous bases).
A hard-masked genome (Ensembl dna_rm) replaces repeats with N, so every junction touching a repeat is skipped: 19% of the chr15 test junctions. See reports/2026-11-11-masked-bases-audit.md.

Caches. JCAST keeps two caches in the user cache directory, or in --cache_dir:

the GTF, read into a table: about 2 GB for GENCODE. The first run on a GTF builds it, about 5 minutes for GENCODE; later runs read it in seconds. A changed GTF gets a new cache.
the UniProt API’s answers, used without --uniprot.

<gtf>.cached files written by earlier versions next to the GTF are no longer used and can be deleted.
A junction that raises an error gets the fate exception in junctions.tsv, with the error in fate_detail, and the run continues. Its traceback is in logfile.log, and the console reports how many junctions failed.
Tier 4 contains products truncated at a stop codon. Alternative C-termini at an annotated stop codon go to psq_T1_alt_cterm.fasta instead. A stop codon that the annotation does not support stays in T4, and some of these may still be genuine. Treat T4 outputs as candidates for follow-up validation, not as confirmed identifications.

title: JCAST - Junction Centric Alternative Splicing Translator
text:
About JCAST
JCAST (Junction Centric Alternative Splicing Translator) is a Python software that takes in splicing events from RNA sequencing data to create custom protein sequence databases for protein isoform analysis.
JCAST attempts to create small protein sequence databases that contain only likely sequences in mass spectrometry experiment samples to avoid runaway database size inflation.
To do so, JCAST selects likely translatable alternative splice junctions, translates each in its annotated reading frame, then joins the translated variant sequences to full-length canonical sequences.



JCAST Workflow

title: Change Log
text:
A hardening release. It corrects how junctions are translated and tiered, adds a few options, and makes runs faster and easier to reproduce. The output changes: re-run any analysis made with v0.3.5a, in particular if it used retained-intron output, C-terminal events or the lower tiers. The CHANGELOG has every change, with its effect on the test data.
Translation and tiers:

The coding-region bounds come from the start and stop codons. Events entirely in UTRs are skipped, with their own fate.
Retained-intron slices no longer include the flanking exons twice.
Each slice is translated in its own annotated reading frame. The three-frame guess and Tier 3 (psq_T3*.fasta) are removed.
A slice ending at an annotated alternative stop codon, or starting at an annotated alternative start codon, is a new class, T1 ALT TERMINUS, written to psq_T1_alt_cterm.fasta, psq_T1_alt_nterm.fasta and psq_T1_alt_both.fasta.
Joining to the canonical is stricter: a complete end is not joined, and the 7-residue anchors must occur once, in order.

New:

--uniprot FASTA: take canonical sequences from a downloaded UniProt FASTA instead of the UniProt API.
About 25× faster on a whole genome. -p N also translates junctions in N processes.
junctions.tsv records each junction’s fate. The log is short and ends with a summary; -v adds each junction’s steps.
When no transcript passes the canonical filter, the GTF canonical falls back to GENCODE’s Ensembl_canonical transcript.

Changed:

-r N keeps junctions with at least N reads. The default, -r 1, keeps every junction; use -m to fit a cutoff.
A run refuses an output directory that already holds JCAST output (use --overwrite).
One failing junction no longer stops the run.
Caches are kept in the user cache directory (--cache_dir), not next to the GTF.
-s works with only some of the five rMATS files in the folder. With -m, the model still fits on every rMATS file present.
--mask is deprecated and ignored. --g_or_ln is removed.
Requires Python 3.11 or later.

title: Change Log
text:
v0.3.5a

JCAST will now skip a junction if the nucleotide sequence contains masked bases
Added the –mask argument to determine masked nucleotide letters (default: NnXx)
Added an option to translate only a subset of splice types (MXE, RI, SE, A3SS, A5SS) with the -s argument

title: Change Log
text:
v0.3.5

Fixed an issue where a small number of slices were not translated.
Fixed an issue where JCAST quits if the model flag is not set.

title: Change Log
text:
v0.3.2

The -q –qvalue option now works by including splice junctions within the specified range. To preserve the previous behavior, use -q 0.01 1. The default -q 0 1 disables filtering.
The -c –canonical argument now defaults to False. To preserve prior behaviors, manually set the -c flag to translate canonical proteins detected in the RNA-seq experiments even if isoform translation failes
The -c –canonical argument now will translate a canonical sequence even if a splice event has low skipped junction counts or falls outside of the specified fdr range
JCAST now automatically models the likely translatable junction count threshold through the -m –model argument. Previously this was done manually then set as an integer (minimal read count) using the -r –read argument.
The skipped junction counts used for modeling now consider the sum of all biological and technical replicates rather than the minimum

title: Change Log

Fixed issues where Gencode GTF files without transcript_biotype annotations could not be read

title: Frequently Asked Questions
text:
A: With --uniprot, search jcast_uniprot_merged.fasta: Swiss-Prot plus the new T1 and T1 alternative-terminus isoforms. Otherwise, append psq_T1.fasta (and, if you want annotated alternative termini, psq_T1_alt_cterm.fasta / psq_T1_alt_nterm.fasta) to either psq_canonical.fasta (if you used -c) or your existing Swiss-Prot canonical database, and search that combined file in your MS pipeline. Lower-tier (T2/T4) and orphan outputs contain frameshifted or truncated sequences and should be interpreted with caution.



A: JCAST reads an unaltered rMATS output folder: one file per splice type, named exactly MXE.MATS.JC.txt, SE.MATS.JC.txt, RI.MATS.JC.txt, A3SS.MATS.JC.txt and A5SS.MATS.JC.txt. Only the files of the splice types selected with -s must be there. With -m, the cutoff is fitted on every one of these files that is present.



A: Yes. JCAST reads GENCODE’s transcript_type as transcript_biotype. When no transcript of a gene passes the canonical filter, it uses the transcript GENCODE tags Ensembl_canonical (see the Documentation).



A: No. From v0.4.0, the parsed GTF is cached in the user cache directory, or in --cache_dir. <gtf>.cached files written by earlier versions are no longer used and can be deleted.



A: Open an issue or a pull request on https://github.com/ed-lau/jcast, or contact us at edward.lau@cuanschutz.edu.

title: Frequently Asked Questions
text:
A: With --uniprot, search jcast_uniprot_merged.fasta: Swiss-Prot plus the new T1 and T1 alternative-terminus isoforms. Otherwise, append psq_T1.fasta (and, if you want annotated alternative termini, psq_T1_alt_cterm.fasta / psq_T1_alt_nterm.fasta) to either psq_canonical.fasta (if you used -c) or your existing Swiss-Prot canonical database, and search that combined file in your MS pipeline. Lower-tier (T2/T4) and orphan outputs contain frameshifted or truncated sequences and should be interpreted with caution.



A: JCAST reads an unaltered rMATS output folder: one file per splice type, named exactly MXE.MATS.JC.txt, SE.MATS.JC.txt, RI.MATS.JC.txt, A3SS.MATS.JC.txt and A5SS.MATS.JC.txt. Only the files of the splice types selected with -s must be there. With -m, the cutoff is fitted on every one of these files that is present.



A: Yes. JCAST reads GENCODE’s transcript_type as transcript_biotype. When no transcript of a gene passes the canonical filter, it uses the transcript GENCODE tags Ensembl_canonical (see the Documentation).



A: No. From v0.4.0, the parsed GTF is cached in the user cache directory, or in --cache_dir. <gtf>.cached files written by earlier versions are no longer used and can be deleted.



A: Open an issue or a pull request on https://github.com/ed-lau/jcast, or contact us at edward.lau@cuanschutz.edu.

title: Quick Start
text:
JCAST requires Python 3.11 or later. It is tested on Python 3.11 to 3.15, on macOS and Linux.
JCAST can be installed from PyPI via pip. We recommend using a virtual environment.
$ pip install jcast






Note



The optional graphical interface (pip install 'jcast[gui]') is an early preview: it opens a window with placeholder pages and cannot run JCAST yet. Use the command line.

title: Quick Start
text:
Running JCAST
Launch JCAST as a module (Usage/Help):
$ python -m jcast
Alternatively:
$ jcast
Example command:
$ python -m jcast \
    /data/encode_human_pancreas/rmats \
    /data/gtf/Homo_sapiens.GRCh38.89.gtf \
    /data/genome/Homo_sapiens.GRCh38.dna.primary_assembly.fa \
    -o encode_human_pancreas \
    -q 0 1 \
    -r 1 -m -c \
    --uniprot /data/uniprot/uniprot_sprot_human_isoforms_2026_04.fasta.gz \
    -p 8
The output directory is created if needed. A directory that already holds JCAST output is refused, so two runs never mix; pass --overwrite to replace that output. See the Documentation for the options, how to download the UniProt FASTA for --uniprot, and the output files.

Test data
The source repository holds a small test set: an rMATS sample and the human chromosome 15 genome and GTF. To run JCAST on it and write the results to the Desktop:
$ git clone https://github.com/ed-lau/jcast
$ cd jcast
$ python -m jcast \
    tests/data/rmats \
    tests/data/genome/Homo_sapiens.GRCh38.89.chromosome.15.gtf \
    tests/data/genome/Homo_sapiens.GRCh38.dna.chromosome.15.fa.gz \
    -o ~/Desktop/jcast_smoke
To run the tests from the same checkout (about 3 minutes):
$ pip install -e '.[test]'
$ pytest -m 'not network'

title: Quick Start
text:
Example Usage
The following is an example using JCAST to generate custom databases from ENCODE public RNA-seq dataset to generate a cardiac-specific database with JCAST.

Download RNA-Seq from ENCODE:
As an example, we will download the .fastq files from ENCODE adult human heart dataset 1 and dataset 2.


Align the FASTQ files to a reference genome
Read alignment can be performed using STAR >= v.2.5.0, e.g.,:
$ STAR --runThreadN 10 --genomeDir path/to/GRCh38/STARindex --sjdbGTFfile path/to/Homo_sapiens.gtf --sjdbOverhang 100 --readFilesIn ./ENCFF781VGS.fastq.gz ./ENCFF466ZAS.fastq.gz --readFilesCommand zcat --outSAMtype BAM SortedByCoordinate --outFileNamePrefix ./STAR_aligned/b1t1/
$ STAR --runThreadN 10 --genomeDir path/to/GRCh38/STARindex --sjdbGTFfile path/to/Homo_sapiens.gtf --sjdbOverhang 100 --readFilesIn ./ENCFF731CDK.fastq.gz ./ENCFF429YOS.fastq.gz --readFilesCommand zcat --outSAMtype BAM SortedByCoordinate --outFileNamePrefix ./STAR_aligned/b2t1/
Note: Arguments including runThreadN and sjdbOverhang should be customized to suit your system and data files. Please refer to the STAR documentations for details.


Identify transcript splice junctions
Splice junctions can be found using rMATS with the .bam files following STAR. Please refer to the rMATS instructions for latest commands. The following example was tested using rmats-turbo-0.1 running in Docker and using rMATS v.4.1.0/Python 3.7. Support for stringtie assembled transcripts will be implemented in a future version.


Set up a Virtual Environment for rMATS turbo 0.1 in Python 2.7 (only if needed)


Install the rMATS image
Follow instructions from rMATS and docker specific to your OS. E.g.:
$ sudo docker load -i rmats-turbo-0.1.tar


Prepare the /rMATS subdirectory
Copy the individual .bam files from STAR into the rMATS subdirectory and rename them b1t1.bam, b1t2.bam, b2t1.bam, b2t2.bam, etc. Copy the GTF file from the Genomes folder as GRCm38.gtf. Write a b1.txt file with a text editor containing the following docker virtual directories:
/data/b1t1.bam,/data/b1t2.bam
Write a b2.txt file
/data/b2t1.bam,/data/b2t2.bam
Go back to the data directory and run the rMATS image. The -v flag mounts the host directory into the docker container at /data, which corresponds to the visual directories in the b1.txt and b2.txt files.
$ sudo docker run -v path/to/data/directory:/data rmats:turbo01 --b1 /data/b1.txt --b2 /data/b2.txt --gtf /data/GRCh38.gtf --od /data/output -t paired  --nthread 4 --readLength 101 --anchorLength 1






Note



Note: Arguments including nThread, readLength, and anchorLength should be customized to suit your system and data files. Please refer to the rMATS documentations for details.


Run the JCAST Python program specifying the path to the rMATS output directory, the genome sequence, as well as the GTF annotation file:
$ python -m jcast path/to/rMATS/output/encode_human_heart/ path/to/gtf/Homo_sapiens.GRCh38.89.gtf path/to/genome/Homo_sapiens.GRCh38.dna.primary_assembly.fa -o encode_human_heart -m -c
